countries.s: Bhutan measures national progress with an index called Gross National Happiness.
countries.e: Bhutan's government uses Gross National Happiness, which weighs wellbeing, culture, environment and good governance alongside economic growth.

countries.s: In Bulgaria, nodding your head up and down traditionally means "no".
countries.e: In Bulgaria (and parts of Albania and Greece), the meanings of nodding and shaking the head are traditionally reversed compared with most of the world.

countries.s: Iceland has no standing army.
countries.e: Iceland is a NATO member but has no army of its own. Its defence relies on its Coast Guard, a peacekeeping unit and agreements with allies.

countries.s: Costa Rica abolished its army in 1948.
countries.e: After a short civil war, President José Figueres Ferrer abolished the military in 1948, and the 1949 constitution made it permanent. The money went to education and healthcare instead.

countries.s: In Japan, leaving a tip at a restaurant is expected, as in the USA.
countries.e: Tipping is uncommon in Japan. Good service is considered part of the job, and staff may even chase you to return money you left behind.

countries.s: Finland has an estimated 3 million saunas for a population of about 5.5 million people.
countries.e: The sauna is central to Finnish life. There are saunas in homes, offices, and even the Finnish parliament.

countries.s: The Great Wall of China is visible from the Moon with the naked eye.
countries.e: The wall is very long but only a few metres wide. From the Moon, about 384,000 km away, it is far too narrow to see. Even from low Earth orbit it is extremely hard to spot.

countries.s: Nepal's national flag is the only national flag that is not a rectangle.
countries.e: Nepal's flag is made of two stacked pennants (triangles). Its constitution even includes precise geometric instructions for drawing it.

countries.s: In Spain, people traditionally eat 12 grapes at midnight on New Year's Eve, one with each chime of the clock.
countries.e: The Twelve Grapes tradition is meant to bring good luck for each month of the new year. Many people watch the clock in Madrid's Puerta del Sol on TV.

countries.s: During the Indian festival of Holi, people throw brightly coloured powder and water at each other.
countries.e: Holi celebrates the arrival of spring and the victory of good over evil. It's celebrated across India and Nepal, and increasingly worldwide.

countries.s: The traditional Ethiopian calendar has 13 months.
countries.e: It has 12 months of 30 days plus a 13th month, Pagume, of 5 or 6 days. It also runs about 7 to 8 years behind the Gregorian calendar.

countries.s: In Saudi Arabia, the weekend falls on Friday and Saturday.
countries.e: Saudi Arabia moved its weekend from Thursday–Friday to Friday–Saturday in 2013. Friday is the main day of congregational prayer in Islam.

countries.s: Sydney is the capital of Australia.
countries.e: The capital is Canberra, a planned city chosen as a compromise between rivals Sydney and Melbourne. Parliament first met there in 1927.

countries.s: South Korea officially switched to the international way of counting age in 2023.
countries.e: Traditionally a baby was counted as 1 year old at birth and everyone aged a year on New Year's Day. A 2023 law made international age the standard for official use.

countries.s: Denmark's flag is often cited as the oldest national flag still in continuous use.
countries.e: Legend says the Dannebrog fell from the sky during a battle in 1219. Its design has been in use since at least the 14th century.

countries.s: Mongolia is the most sparsely populated sovereign country in the world.
countries.e: With about 2 people per square kilometre, Mongolia has the lowest population density of any independent country. Around 30% of Mongolians are nomadic or semi-nomadic.

countries.s: In Thailand, touching someone's head is usually considered rude.
countries.e: The head is traditionally seen as the most sacred part of the body, while pointing your feet at people or religious images is considered disrespectful.

countries.s: Vatican City is the smallest country in the world by area.
countries.e: Vatican City covers about 0.49 km², smaller than many city parks, and has a population of only a few hundred people.

countries.s: Russia spans five time zones.
countries.e: Russia spans 11 time zones, from Kaliningrad in the west to Kamchatka in the far east.

countries.s: The Maldives is the world's lowest-lying country, with an average ground level of about 1.5 metres above sea level.
countries.e: This makes the Maldives one of the countries most threatened by rising sea levels.

food.e: Bananas contain potassium, a tiny fraction of which is radioactive potassium-40. The dose is harmless, and the 'banana equivalent dose' is used as a light-hearted unit of radiation.

food.s: Properly sealed honey can stay edible for an extremely long time.
food.e: Honey has very little water and is acidic, so most bacteria and moulds can't grow in it. It may crystallise, but that doesn't mean it has gone bad.

food.s: Botanically, a tomato is a vegetable.
food.e: Botanically, tomatoes are fruits, specifically berries, because they develop from a flower and contain seeds. In cooking they are treated as vegetables.

food.s: Peanuts are not true nuts; they are legumes, related to beans and peas.
food.e: Peanuts grow underground in pods, like other legumes. Botanically, 'nuts' are hard-shelled fruits like hazelnuts and chestnuts.

food.s: Most "wasabi" served outside Japan is actually horseradish dyed green.
food.e: Real wasabi is rare and expensive to grow, so most restaurant wasabi is a mix of horseradish, mustard and green colouring.

food.s: Fortune cookies are a traditional dessert in China.
food.e: Fortune cookies became popular in the United States in the early 20th century and are thought to come from Japanese crackers. They are rarely seen in China.

food.s: Cashew nuts grow attached to the bottom of a fruit called the cashew apple.
food.e: Each cashew nut hangs below a juicy 'cashew apple'. The shell contains an irritating oil, so cashews are always sold shelled and processed.

food.s: Saffron, made from the stigmas of crocus flowers, is one of the most expensive spices in the world by weight.
food.e: Every flower yields only three thin stigmas, each picked by hand. It takes roughly 150,000 flowers to make a kilogram of saffron.

food.s: The holes in Swiss cheese are made by mice nibbling it while it ages.
food.e: The holes ('eyes') come from carbon dioxide bubbles released by bacteria during ripening. Tiny hay particles in the milk also help the bubbles form.

food.s: Potatoes were first domesticated in the Andes of South America.
food.e: Potatoes were domesticated in what is now southern Peru and north-western Bolivia thousands of years ago. They reached Europe only in the 16th century.

food.s: The croissant descends from the Austrian kipferl.
food.e: The croissant is a symbol of France, but it grew out of the Viennese kipferl, popularised by Viennese bakeries in Paris in the 1830s and 40s.

food.s: Coffee beans are the seeds of a fruit.
food.e: Coffee 'beans' are the seeds inside the red or purple fruit of the coffee plant, often called coffee cherries.

food.s: Traditional Italian carbonara is made with cream.
food.e: Traditional carbonara uses egg, hard cheese (pecorino or parmesan), cured pork (guanciale) and black pepper. The creaminess comes from the eggs and cheese.

food.s: White chocolate contains lots of cocoa solids.
food.e: White chocolate is made from cocoa butter, sugar and milk. It contains no cocoa solids, which is why it isn't brown.

food.s: Chocolate (cacao) was first used in Mesoamerica, where it was often drunk as a bitter beverage.
food.e: The Olmec, Maya and Aztec peoples drank cacao, often spiced and unsweetened. Cacao beans were even used as a currency by the Aztecs.

laws.s: Singapore has banned the sale of chewing gum since 1992.
laws.e: The ban was introduced partly because discarded gum was damaging public places and train doors. Therapeutic gum, such as nicotine gum, is allowed from pharmacies.
laws.w: Chewing gum sales ban in Singapore

laws.s: In Switzerland, owning just one guinea pig is not allowed, because they are social animals.
laws.e: Swiss animal welfare law requires social animals like guinea pigs to be kept with companions of their own kind.

laws.s: In Germany, most shops are legally required to close on Sundays.
laws.e: Sundays and public holidays are protected as days of rest. There are exceptions for bakeries, petrol stations, train stations and some special shopping Sundays.

laws.s: Estonia was the first country to use internet voting in legally binding nationwide elections.
laws.e: Estonians could first vote online in the 2005 local elections, using their national digital ID cards. Today a large share of votes is cast online.

laws.s: Voting in federal elections is compulsory for adult citizens in Australia.
laws.e: Since 1924, Australian citizens aged 18 and over must enrol and vote. Turnout is usually above 90%.

laws.s: Most countries in the world drive on the left side of the road.
laws.e: Only about a third of countries drive on the left, including the UK, India, Japan and Australia. Most countries drive on the right.

laws.s: New Zealand was the first self-governing country to give women the right to vote in national elections.
laws.e: New Zealand women won the vote in 1893 after a campaign led by Kate Sheppard, whose portrait appears on the NZ$10 note.

laws.s: Japan lowered its legal age of adulthood from 20 to 18 in 2022.
laws.e: Since April 2022, 18-year-olds in Japan can sign contracts and marry without parental consent. The drinking and smoking age stays at 20.

laws.s: In Sweden, the law lets anyone walk, and even camp for a night, on most private land, as long as they respect nature and owners.
laws.e: This 'right of public access' (allemansrätten) is a deep Nordic tradition. Norway and Finland have similar rights.

laws.s: France has a law giving many employees a 'right to disconnect' from work emails outside working hours.
laws.e: Since 2017, French companies with 50 or more employees must agree on rules that protect workers from out-of-hours emails and messages.

languages.s: Papua New Guinea has more living languages than any other country, over 800.
languages.e: Its rugged mountains and isolated valleys allowed hundreds of languages to develop separately. Tok Pisin, English and Hiri Motu are widely used to bridge them.
The Eighth Schedule lists 22 languages, including Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Marathi and Urdu. Hundreds more are spoken across the country.
languages.w: Eighth Schedule to the Constitution of India

languages.s: Spanish has more native speakers than any other language.
languages.e: Mandarin Chinese has the most native speakers, about 900 million or more. Spanish is second, with nearly 500 million. English has the most total speakers when second-language speakers are counted.
languages.w: List of languages by number of native speakers

languages.s: On La Gomera in the Canary Islands, people use a whistled language called Silbo Gomero.
languages.e: Silbo turns Spanish into whistles that can carry across deep valleys for several kilometres. It's taught in local schools and is recognised by UNESCO.

languages.s: The Korean alphabet, Hangul, was deliberately invented in the 15th century.
languages.e: King Sejong the Great and his scholars created Hangul in 1443 so ordinary people could read and write easily. Korea celebrates Hangul Day every October.

languages.s: The word 'robot' was first used in a Czech play.
languages.e: It comes from Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R. and the Czech word 'robota', meaning forced labour. His brother Josef suggested the word.

languages.s: The Hawaiian alphabet has only 13 letters.
languages.e: It has 5 vowels and 8 consonants, including the ʻokina, a glottal stop. Words like 'aloha' and 'ukulele' come from Hawaiian.

languages.s: Basque is a language isolate, unrelated to any other living language.
languages.e: Basque, spoken in parts of Spain and France, is thought to predate the arrival of Indo-European languages in Europe. Its origins remain a mystery.

languages.s: Esperanto is the official language of several countries.
languages.e: Esperanto was invented in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof as an easy international language. It has an active community worldwide, but no country uses it as an official language.

languages.s: English words like 'shampoo', 'bungalow' and 'jungle' come from Indian languages.
languages.e: Shampoo comes from Hindi 'chāmpo' (to press or massage), bungalow from 'bangla' (Bengal-style house), and jungle from 'jangal'.
languages.w: List of English words of Hindi or Urdu origin

languages.s: Arabic is written from right to left, but its numbers are read from left to right.
languages.e: Arabic text runs right to left, but multi-digit numbers are written with the most significant digit on the left, just as in English.

languages.s: In Mandarin Chinese, the same syllable can mean completely different things depending on its tone.
languages.e: Mandarin has four main tones. For example, 'mā' can mean 'mother' while 'mǎ' can mean 'horse'.

languages.s: Sign language is universal, so deaf people everywhere use the same signs.
languages.e: There are hundreds of sign languages. British Sign Language and American Sign Language are very different, even though both countries mostly speak English.

languages.s: Finnish and Hungarian are distantly related languages.
languages.e: Both belong to the Uralic language family, along with Estonian. Unlike most European languages, they are not Indo-European.

geography.s: Russia's land area is larger than the entire surface area of Pluto.
geography.e: Russia covers about 17.1 million km², and Pluto's whole surface is about 16.7 million km².

geography.s: Africa is the only continent crossed by both the Equator and the Prime Meridian.
geography.e: The Equator and the Prime Meridian meet in the Gulf of Guinea, off the coast of West Africa.

geography.s: Mount Everest is the tallest mountain on Earth when measured from base to peak.
geography.e: Everest has the highest summit above sea level, at 8,849 m. Measured from its base on the ocean floor, Hawaii's Mauna Kea is about 10,200 m tall.

geography.s: Canada has the longest coastline of any country.
geography.e: Thanks to its thousands of Arctic islands, Canada's coastline is over 200,000 km long by common measures, far more than any other country.

geography.s: The shores of the Dead Sea are the lowest land on Earth, about 430 metres below sea level.
geography.e: The Dead Sea is also so salty that people float effortlessly in it. Its level has been dropping for decades.

geography.s: The Sahara is the largest desert in the world.
geography.e: A desert is defined by low rainfall, not heat. Antarctica is the largest desert, followed by the Arctic. The Sahara is the largest hot desert.

geography.s: Russia's Lake Baikal holds about a fifth of the world's unfrozen surface fresh water.
geography.e: Baikal is the deepest lake on Earth, at over 1,600 m, and one of the oldest, at about 25 million years.

geography.s: France has more time zones than any other country.
geography.e: Because of overseas territories like French Polynesia, Réunion and New Caledonia, France spans 12 time zones (13 including its Antarctic claim).

geography.s: Istanbul is a city on two continents, Europe and Asia.
geography.e: The Bosphorus strait divides Istanbul between Europe and Asia, and millions of people cross between the two every day.

geography.s: Brazil borders every South American country except Chile and Ecuador.
geography.e: Brazil is so large that it touches 10 of the other 12 South American countries, plus French Guiana.

geography.s: The Danube flows through or along more countries than any other river: 10.
geography.e: It passes Germany, Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, Moldova and Ukraine, and four capital cities.

geography.s: Indonesia is made up of more than 17,000 islands.
geography.e: Indonesia is the world's largest archipelagic country. About 6,000 of its islands are inhabited.

geography.s: There's a point in the South Pacific so far from land that the nearest humans are often astronauts on the International Space Station.
geography.e: Point Nemo, the oceanic pole of inaccessibility, is about 2,700 km from the nearest land. The ISS, about 400 km up, is often closer.

geography.s: Alaska is both the westernmost and the easternmost US state.
geography.e: Alaska's Aleutian Islands cross the 180° meridian, so some of them lie in the Eastern Hemisphere.
India lies entirely north of the Equator. It's the Tropic of Cancer that crosses India, through eight states.
